title: What Moves Exchange Rates
short: Tastes, relative incomes, relative price levels and relative interest rates shift the demand for and supply of a currency.
trouble: Students expect higher U.S. inflation to strengthen the dollar. It makes U.S. goods dearer and tends to weaken the dollar.

blocks.html: Now shift the curves in the The Foreign Exchange Market. The usual shifters connect to ideas from earlier units: real interest rates and inflation.

The main shifters of demand for and supply of a currency: tastes for a country's goods, relative incomes, relative price levels (inflation) and relative real interest rates, plus speculation and central bank purchases. For the dollar: higher U.S. real interest rates or higher foreign incomes raise demand for dollars (appreciation); higher U.S. incomes or higher U.S. inflation push the dollar down (depreciation).

Ask who now wants more or fewer dollars. If U.S. real interest rates rise, foreign savers want U.S. bonds and must buy dollars: demand rises. If Europeans get richer, they buy more of everything, U.S. goods included: demand for dollars rises. If Americans get richer, they buy more imports and sell dollars to do it: supply rises. If U.S. prices rise faster than Europe's, U.S. goods look expensive: Europeans want fewer dollars and Americans supply more to buy cheaper European goods. Both push the dollar down.

blocks.title: Higher U.S. inflation
blocks.q: Inflation in the United States runs well above Europe's. What happens to the dollar against the euro?
steps: U.S. goods get pricier compared with European goods.
Europeans demand fewer dollars, and Americans supply more dollars to buy European goods.
The dollar depreciates; the euro appreciates.

blocks.title: A demand shift with numbers
blocks.q: Demand for dollars is $Q_D = 150 - 100e$ and supply is $Q_S = -30 + 100e$, so $e = 0.90$. U.S. interest rates rise and demand grows by 20 at every rate. Find the new rate.
steps: Set it equal to supply: $170 - 100e = -30 + 100e$, so $200 = 200e$.
$e = 1.00$ euro per dollar: the dollar appreciated from 0.90.

blocks.html: Expecting higher U.S. inflation to strengthen the dollar. It makes U.S. goods dearer and tends to weaken the dollar. Check: would foreigners want more U.S. goods, or fewer, after U.S. prices jump?
